name: King's Pawn Opening
blurb: The most direct first move. The pawn takes the centre and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop.
history:
The name is purely descriptive: White advances the pawn in front of the king two squares. In the older English notation the move was written P-K4, and it is the first move of most of the games analysed in the earliest books on modern chess, from around 1500.

Bobby Fischer opened with it almost every time he had White and called it "best by test". When he played something else in the sixth game of his 1972 world championship match with Boris Spassky, it was news.
ideas: Follow up by developing knights before bishops.
Aim to castle within the first ten moves.
The e4 pawn is undefended at first, so expect it to be attacked.

name: Open Game
blurb: Black mirrors White and claims an equal share of the centre. Most classical openings start here.
history:
Also called the Double King's Pawn Opening. It is "open" because with both e-pawns advanced the centre pawns tend to be exchanged early, leaving open files and diagonals for the pieces. The name is a pair with the Closed Game, 1.d4 d5, where that happens far less easily.

Until late in the nineteenth century nearly every serious game began this way. The showpieces of that era, Adolf Anderssen's Immortal Game of 1851 and his Evergreen Game of 1852, are both Open Games.
ideas: Your e5 pawn will be attacked by Nf3. Be ready to defend it with ...Nc6 or ...d6, or to hit back at e4 with ...Nf6.
Develop the king's knight and bishop, then castle.
Don't bring the queen out early.

name: King's Knight Opening
blurb: White develops a piece and attacks the e5 pawn at once. It is the main road into the Italian, the Ruy Lopez and the Scotch.
history: A descriptive name: White brings out the knight on the king's side at move two. It has been the main second move since the first books on modern chess, and almost every famous Open Game opening, the Italian, the Ruy Lopez, the Scotch and Petrov's Defense among them, starts from here.
ideas: Nf3 develops with a threat, so Black must react.
It prepares short castling.
If Black defends badly, for example with ...f6, Nxe5 is often strong.

name: King's Knight: Normal Variation
blurb: The natural defence. The knight protects e5 and develops at the same time.
history:
Called the normal variation simply because it is the reply nearly everyone plays. The Portuguese writer Pedro Damiano judged it the best way to defend the e5 pawn in his book of 1512, and that verdict has stood ever since.

By a quirk of history Damiano's own name is attached to the reply he called the worst, 2...f6, now known as the Damiano Defense.
ideas: ...Nc6 is better than ...f6, which weakens your king, and more active than ...d6.
Next develop the other knight or the f8 bishop.
Watch the f7 square once White's bishop comes to c4.

name: Italian Game
blurb: The bishop takes the diagonal that points at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp.
history:
Named for the Italian masters of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, above all Giulio Cesare Polerio and Gioachino Greco, whose manuscripts are full of games with this bishop move. It is among the oldest openings on record and appears in the Göttingen manuscript of around 1500.

After a century of being thought too tame for master play it came back in the 2010s, when the world's best players took up its slow lines to get away from the heavily analysed Ruy Lopez.
ideas: Castle early, then prepare d4 with c3.
Ng5 can attack f7 a second time if Black is careless.
Keep the bishop on the a2 to g8 diagonal; retreat to b3 if it is chased.

name: Ruy Lopez
blurb: The bishop pressures the knight that defends e5. White keeps the tension and builds slowly.
history:
Named after Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest who analysed it in his chess book of 1561. In most languages it is simply the Spanish Opening or Spanish Game. The move itself is older than López and is already in the Göttingen manuscript of around 1500.

It has been the most heavily studied of the Open Games since the middle of the nineteenth century. One of its best-known moments came in London in 2000, when Vladimir Kramnik used the Berlin Defense, soon nicknamed the Berlin Wall, to keep Garry Kasparov from winning a single game with White and took his world title.
ideas: Taking on c6 does not win the e5 pawn straight away; Black has ...Qd4 tricks.
Castle, play Re1, then c3 and d4.
If Black plays ...a6, retreat with Ba4 and keep the pin idea alive.

name: Scotch Game
blurb: White opens the centre immediately instead of preparing it. The position clears quickly and pieces come out fast.
history:
The name comes from a correspondence match between the chess clubs of Edinburgh and London that began in 1824. London tried the opening first, Edinburgh took it up later in the same match and won with it, and it has been the Scotch ever since.

It fell out of fashion for most of the twentieth century until Garry Kasparov brought it back against Anatoly Karpov in their 1990 world championship match.
ideas: After ...exd4, recapture with Nxd4.
You get open lines for both bishops.
Be ready for ...Qh4 and ...Bc5 ideas against your centre.

name: Petrov's Defense
blurb: Instead of defending e5, Black counterattacks e4. It is solid and hard to break down.
history:
Named after Alexander Petrov, the strongest Russian player of the first half of the nineteenth century, who worked on it with Carl Jaenisch in the 1840s. It is also called the Russian Defense or Russian Game.

Black answers the attack on e5 by attacking e4 in return. It has a reputation for being very hard to beat, and it has been a main defence of world-class players such as Vladimir Kramnik and Fabiano Caruana, who relied on it in his 2018 world championship match with Magnus Carlsen.
ideas: After Nxe5, play ...d6 first to chase the knight, and only then take on e4.
Taking on e4 immediately runs into Qe2 and can lose a piece.
The positions are often symmetrical, so development speed matters.

name: Philidor Defense
blurb: Black supports e5 with a pawn. It is sturdy but shuts in the f8 bishop.
history:
Named after François-André Danican Philidor, the French master and opera composer who was the best player of the eighteenth century. In his 1749 book he recommended 2...d6 because it keeps the f-pawn free to advance; he is the author of the saying that pawns are the soul of chess.

The most famous game in the opening went badly for Black. In 1858 Paul Morphy beat the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard in a box at the Paris opera in seventeen moves, a game still shown to beginners as a model of fast development.
ideas: Develop with ...Nf6, ...Be7 and castle.
Don't pin the f3 knight with ...Bg4 too early; there are tactics against it.
Expect a slightly cramped but solid position.

name: Wayward Queen Attack: 2...Nc6
blurb: White's early queen attacks e5 and eyes f7. Defending the pawn with the knight is the first half of the cure.
history:
The queen comes out on the second move, against all the usual advice, which is where the name comes from. The opening is also known as the Parham Attack, after the American master Bernard Parham who championed it, and less kindly as the Patzer Opening.

It is rare in serious chess, but Hikaru Nakamura played it in grandmaster tournaments in 2005. This line, 2...Nc6, is Black's most natural answer: it defends the e5 pawn the queen is attacking and develops a piece.
ideas: Never answer Qh5 with ...g6 straight away; that drops the e5 pawn with check.
After Bc4 the threat is mate on f7. Block it with ...g6, which now also hits the queen.
Then develop with ...Nf6 and gain time on the queen.

name: Sicilian Defense
blurb: Black fights for d4 from the side instead of matching White in the centre. The positions are unbalanced from move one.
history:
The opening was analysed in Italy in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, by Giulio Cesare Polerio and by the Sicilian priest Pietro Carrera among others. The English name dates from 1813, when Jacob Sarratt translated an old Italian manuscript that called it "il gioco siciliano", the Sicilian game.

It was a sideline for a long time. Since the middle of the twentieth century it has been the most popular and most successful answer to 1.e4 at every level, and the favourite weapon of Bobby Fischer and Garry Kasparov.
ideas: If White plays d4, trade your c-pawn for it and keep two centre pawns.
Develop with ...d6 or ...Nc6, then ...Nf6.
The half-open c-file is your long-term asset.

name: French Defense
blurb: Black prepares ...d5 with pawn support. The structure is solid; the price is a passive c8 bishop.
history:
Named after a correspondence match between the cities of London and Paris in 1834. The Paris team answered 1.e4 with 1...e6 and won, and the defence has been French ever since.

It gives a solid but slightly cramped game in which Black's light-squared bishop is the problem piece. Mikhail Botvinnik, Viktor Korchnoi and Wolfgang Uhlmann, who played almost nothing else against 1.e4, are its best-known champions.
ideas: Play ...d5 next and challenge e4.
If White advances with e5, attack the pawn chain at its base with ...c5.
Find a job for the light-squared bishop before it gets locked in.

name: Scandinavian Defense
blurb: Black challenges e4 on the very first move and forces the game into its own territory.
history:
Also called the Center Counter Defense. It is the opening of the oldest recorded game of modern chess, played in Valencia around 1475 and preserved in the Catalan poem Scachs d'amor. The present name comes from the Scandinavian masters who analysed and played it in the late nineteenth century, among them the Swede Ludvig Collijn.

It was thought a little too simple for top-level chess until Viswanathan Anand chose it against Garry Kasparov in their 1995 world championship match and got a good position out of the opening.
ideas: After exd5 Qxd5, expect Nc3 to hit your queen. Retreat to a5 or d6.
Develop quickly to make up for the queen's lost time.
A setup with ...c6 gives the queen a way home.

name: Scandinavian: 2.exd5
blurb: Take the pawn. It is the only move that asks Black a question, and it is free development after the recapture.
history: White simply takes the pawn, which is what happens in nearly every Scandinavian. The capture costs nothing, and declining it gives Black an easy game. The choice then passes back to Black: recapture at once with the queen, or play 2...Nf6 and take the pawn back with the knight a move later.
ideas: After ...Qxd5, play Nc3 and gain a move on the queen.
Don't defend e4 with f3; it weakens your king and blocks the knight.
Then develop normally: d4, Nf3, bishops out, castle.

name: Queen's Pawn Opening
blurb: The other main first move. The pawn is defended by the queen from the start, which leads to slower, more strategic games.
history:
A descriptive name: White advances the pawn in front of the queen. Unlike the e-pawn after 1.e4, this pawn is protected from the first move, which makes the play slower and harder to open up.

In the attacking chess of the early nineteenth century it was a rarity. It rose with the positional ideas of Wilhelm Steinitz and his followers, and by the 1920s it had become the usual first move in world championship matches.
ideas: c4 often follows, to pressure Black's centre.
Knights usually go to f3 and c3.
Tactics arrive later than in 1.e4 games; build first.

name: Closed Game
blurb: Black matches White in the centre. The d-pawns lock and the fight moves to the squares around them.
history: Also called the Double Queen's Pawn Opening. It is the "closed" counterpart of the Open Game, 1.e4 e5: both d-pawns are defended by their queens, so the centre is hard to break open and the struggle is slower. Most games from here go into the Queen's Gambit.
ideas: Be ready for c4, the Queen's Gambit.
Develop with ...Nf6 and ...e6.
Avoid blocking your c-pawn with ...Nc6 too early; it usually wants to move.

name: Queen's Gambit
blurb: White offers a wing pawn to pull Black's d-pawn away from the centre. It is not a real sacrifice; the pawn can almost always be won back.
history:
One of the oldest openings on record, described in the Göttingen manuscript and in Lucena's book of 1497. A gambit is an opening that offers material for an advantage elsewhere; the word comes from the Italian gambetto, a trip in wrestling, and Ruy López was the first to use it for chess. This one is hardly a real gambit, since Black cannot keep the c-pawn for long.

It became the backbone of top-level chess in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Many people now know the name from the 2020 television series The Queen's Gambit.
ideas: If Black takes, play e3 or e4 and recapture with the bishop.
Develop Nc3 and Nf3 to add pressure on d5.
Don't rush to win the pawn back with your queen.

name: London System
blurb: A setup you can play against almost anything. The bishop comes out before e3 shuts it in.
history:
Named after the London tournament of 1922, where several of the leading players used this bishop development. The English-based master James Mason had played it regularly in the 1880s.

For decades it was considered a dull way to avoid theory. That changed in the 2010s, when Magnus Carlsen and other top players began to use it, and it is now one of the most popular openings at club level because the same setup works against almost anything.
ideas: Build the triangle: pawns on d4, e3 and c3.
Knights to f3 and d2, bishop to d3, then castle.
Watch for ...Qb6 hitting b2 once your bishop has left c1.

name: Giuoco Piano
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5
blurb: Black puts the bishop on its best diagonal and answers White's pressure on f7 with pressure on f2.
history:
Italian for "quiet game", so called to set it apart from the gambits that were the alternative when the name was coined. It was analysed by Damiano in the early sixteenth century and by Gioachino Greco in the seventeenth.

The names Giuoco Piano and Italian Game are often used for the same thing. Strictly, the Giuoco Piano is the Italian Game in which Black answers with the same bishop move.
ideas: Castle soon; your king is the target of Ng5 and Bxf7 ideas.
Meet c3 with ...Nf6, attacking e4 before White gets d4 in comfortably.
After d4 exd4 cxd4, ...Bb4+ saves the bishop with check.

name: Giuoco Piano: 4.c3
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3
blurb: White prepares d4, to build a full pawn centre and push the c5 bishop back.
history:
The oldest plan in the Giuoco Piano: the pawn move prepares d4, building a full pawn centre and hitting Black's bishop. Gioachino Greco's manuscripts of the 1620s contain brilliant attacks from this position, and one sharp line still carries his name, the Greco Attack.

The modern version is slower. White plays d3 first and saves d4 for later, a setup known as the Giuoco Pianissimo, the "very quiet game".
ideas: After d4 exd4, recapture with the c-pawn.
Black's best reply is ...Nf6, hitting e4. Decide in advance: d3 for a quiet game, d4 for a sharp one.
If unsure, castle before opening the centre.

name: Evans Gambit
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4
blurb: White gives up a wing pawn to gain time for c3 and d4.
history:
Named after William Davies Evans, a Welsh sea captain who first played it against Alexander McDonnell in London in 1827. White gives up the b-pawn to gain time for a quick centre.

It was the most feared opening of the nineteenth century and produced Adolf Anderssen's Evergreen Game in 1852. It then lay almost unused for a hundred years, until Garry Kasparov beat Viswanathan Anand with it in twenty-five moves at Riga in 1995.
ideas: After ...Bxb4, play c3 to hit the bishop, then d4.
You are a pawn down, so play fast: develop, castle, open lines.
Ba3 can stop Black from castling.

name: Two Knights Defense
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6
blurb: Black counterattacks e4 instead of copying White. It invites Ng5, so you need to know one line.
history:
A descriptive name: Black has developed both knights. It was analysed by Giulio Cesare Polerio in the late sixteenth century.

It is less a defence than a counterattack, since Black ignores the threat to f7 and attacks e4 instead. David Bronstein argued that it ought to be renamed the Chigorin Counterattack for that reason, after the Russian master Mikhail Chigorin who played it so well.
ideas: Against Ng5, play ...d5. It is the only good way to block the attack on f7.
After exd5, don't recapture with the knight; Nxf7, the Fried Liver, follows. Play ...Na5.
Against a quiet d3, just develop with ...Bc5 or ...Be7.

name: Two Knights: Knight Attack
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5
blurb: Knight and bishop both hit f7. Black has exactly one good defence, and many players don't know it.
history:
The knight moves a second time to attack f7 together with the bishop, which is all the name means. Siegbert Tarrasch, the great teacher of classical principles, dismissed it as a duffer's move because it breaks the rule about moving a piece twice in the opening.

It has turned out to be White's most testing try all the same, and it leads to some of the sharpest and oldest analysis in chess.
ideas: If Black ignores the threat, take on f7 and fork the queen and rook.
After ...d5 exd5 Nxd5, the sacrifice Nxf7 (the Fried Liver) gives a strong attack.
You have moved the knight twice, so if the attack fails you are behind in development.

name: Knight Attack: 4...d5
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 Ng5 d5
blurb: The pawn blocks the bishop's line to f7. It is the only move that holds.
history:
The one good way to shut out the bishop: Black gives up a pawn to block the diagonal to f7. After 5.exd5 the usual move is 5...Na5, analysed by Polerio around 1600.

Recapturing with 5...Nxd5 instead allows the Fried Liver Attack, a knight sacrifice on f7 that drags the black king into the middle of the board. Its name translates the Italian fegatello, and it dates from a game Polerio recorded in Rome around 1610. It is still one of the first traps a new player learns.
ideas: After exd5, play ...Na5 to chase the bishop. Avoid ...Nxd5.
You are a pawn down for a while but gain time against White's pieces.
...h6 next sends the knight back.

name: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6
blurb: Black asks the bishop what it wants straight away. If it retreats, ...b5 is available later to break the pressure.
history:
Named after Paul Morphy of New Orleans, who beat the best players of Europe in 1858 and made 3...a6 popular. He did not invent it, but his success with it did the persuading.

The pawn asks the bishop to decide at once between taking the knight and retreating. It is by far the most common reply to the Ruy Lopez, and the starting point of most of that opening's theory.
ideas: After Bxc6 dxc6, Nxe5 is met by ...Qd4, winning the pawn back.
After Ba4, continue ...Nf6 and ...Be7, then castle.
Keep ...b5 in reserve to push the bishop off the a4 to e8 diagonal.

name: Four Knights Game
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6
blurb: Both sides bring out all four knights before anything else. Solid and easy to play.
history:
A descriptive name: all four knights are developed before anything else. It was common in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and has a reputation for sound, symmetrical positions.

Akiba Rubinstein livened it up for Black with the pawn sacrifice 4.Bb5 Nd4, which still bears his name.
ideas: Continue with Bb5 in Ruy Lopez style, or d4 in Scotch style.
Nothing is hanging and nothing is forced, so clean development decides the game.
Watch for ...Nd4 tricks if you play Bb5.

name: Petrov: 3.Nxe5
blurb: Take the pawn. Black cannot take back on e4 straight away without trouble.
history: The main line: White takes the pawn that Black left undefended. It sets one of the best-known traps in chess. If Black copies with 3...Nxe4, then 4.Qe2 wins material, because the knight cannot move away without exposing the king to a discovered check.
ideas: If Black plays ...Nxe4 at once, Qe2 wins material.
After ...d6, retreat with Nf3. Then ...Nxe4 is fine for Black and you play d4.
The position stays symmetrical, so a lead in development is what you are playing for.

name: Petrov: 3...d6
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6
blurb: Chase the knight first, then take the e4 pawn safely.
history: The right way to play the Petrov: Black first drives the knight away and only then takes on e4, sidestepping the trap that follows an immediate recapture. The positions that result are symmetrical and very solid, which is why the opening has long been a favourite of players who want to neutralise 1.e4 at the highest level.
ideas: After Nf3, play ...Nxe4.
If Qe2 pins your knight, defend it with ...Qe7.
Never take on e4 before ...d6: Qe2 wins material.

name: Bishop's Opening
blurb: The bishop goes to its best square first and leaves the f-pawn free to move.
history:
A descriptive name, and one of the oldest openings there is, analysed by Lucena and by Ruy López. Philidor preferred it to 2.Nf3 because it leaves the f-pawn free to advance.

It disappeared from master chess for most of a century until Bent Larsen revived it in the 1960s. It often turns into a Vienna Game or an Italian Game by a different order of moves.
ideas: It often becomes an Italian Game after Nf3.
d3 and Nc3 give a solid setup.
Against ...Nf6, defend e4 with d3 or Nc3.

name: Vienna Game
blurb: White protects e4 and keeps the f-pawn free for f4.
history:
Named for the players of Vienna who developed it in the middle of the nineteenth century, chief among them Carl Hamppe; it was once known as Hamppe's Opening. Wilhelm Steinitz, who learned his chess in Vienna, added a wild gambit of his own to it.

The idea is to play f4 a move later than in the King's Gambit, with the knight already guarding the centre.
ideas: f4 next gives a King's Gambit style attack with less risk.
Bc4 and d3 give a quieter setup.
Against ...Nf6, f4 is the Vienna Gambit; if ...exf4, e5 chases the knight.

name: King's Gambit
blurb: White offers the f-pawn to pull Black's e-pawn away and open the f-file.
history:
White offers the f-pawn, the pawn beside the king, to pull Black's e-pawn out of the centre and open the f-file. It is among the oldest openings on record and was analysed by Ruy López in 1561.

It ruled the attacking chess of the nineteenth century and produced the Immortal Game, Anderssen against Kieseritzky in London in 1851. After losing to Boris Spassky's King's Gambit in 1960, Bobby Fischer published an article called A Bust to the King's Gambit, claiming to have refuted it. It is still played, mostly by people who enjoy the risk.
ideas: If Black takes, play Nf3 to stop ...Qh4+.
Then Bc4 and castle; the f-file opens toward f7.
Your own king is exposed too. Expect sharp games.

name: Center Game: 2...exd4
blurb: White strikes in the centre at once. Take the pawn.
history:
So called because White opens the centre immediately with 2.d4, and Black's capture is the natural reply. If White takes back with the queen, Black gains time by attacking it with 3...Nc6, which is why the opening has never been popular with masters.

White can instead offer pawns with 3.c3, the Danish Gambit, named after the Danish players who used it in the nineteenth century.
ideas: After Qxd4, play ...Nc6 and gain a move on the queen.
If White offers more pawns with c3, the Danish Gambit, you can decline with ...d5.
Develop fast; White's early queen gives you free moves.

name: Wayward Queen: 3...g6
moves: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6
blurb: With e5 defended, ...g6 blocks the mate on f7 and hits the queen.
history:
Black's standard answer to the threat of Scholar's Mate, the four-move checkmate on f7 that the queen and bishop are aiming at. The pawn blocks the queen's line and chases it away with the next move, and the bishop can later settle on g7.

The mate has been called Scholar's Mate in English since a chess book of 1656. Nearly every player loses to it once and learns this move as the cure.
ideas: After Qf3 the mate threat is back. Play ...Nf6.
Then ...Bg7 and castle; your position is already better.
Look for ...Nd4, hitting the queen and c2.

name: Sicilian: 2.Nf3
blurb: The main move. White develops and prepares d4.
history: The most common second move. The knight prepares d4, which opens the game and leads to the Open Sicilian. White's other choices at this point, such as 2.c3 and 2.Nc3, are grouped together as the Anti-Sicilians because they avoid that main road.
ideas: d4 next opens the position; recapture on d4 with the knight.
You get a lead in development; Black gets an extra centre pawn.
If you prefer quiet play, Bc4 or Bb5 setups are possible.

name: Sicilian: 2...d6
blurb: Black covers e5 and prepares ...Nf6 without being hit by e5.
history: The most popular second move for Black, and the way into two of the most famous Sicilians. The Najdorf is named after the Polish-Argentine grandmaster Miguel Najdorf and was the lifelong choice of Bobby Fischer and Garry Kasparov. The Dragon is said to have been named by the Russian master Fyodor Dus-Chotimirsky in 1901, because the shape of Black's pawns reminded him of the constellation Draco.
ideas: After d4, always take: ...cxd4.
Then ...Nf6 attacks e4 and makes White defend it with Nc3.
Choose your setup afterwards: ...a6 (Najdorf), ...g6 (Dragon) or ...e6.

name: Open Sicilian
blurb: White trades the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn and gets open lines for every piece.
history:
Called open because White exchanges the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn, opening lines for the pieces. White gets faster development and more space; Black gets an extra pawn in the centre and the half-open c-file. That imbalance is why the Sicilian leads to so many decisive games.

Bent Larsen was sceptical, and liked to point out that White is giving up a centre pawn for a wing pawn.
ideas: After ...cxd4, recapture with Nxd4, not Qxd4.
Nc3 next defends e4.
White usually attacks on the kingside; Black plays on the c-file and queenside.

name: Sicilian: Alapin
blurb: White prepares d4 and wants to recapture with a pawn, keeping a full centre.
history:
Named after Semyon Alapin, a Russian master of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with a taste for unusual opening ideas. The pawn supports d4 so that White can build a full centre without allowing the Open Sicilian.

It was long thought harmless and became respectable in the 1980s, largely through the work of Evgeny Sveshnikov. Deep Blue played it in the first game of its 1996 match with Garry Kasparov, the first game a computer won against a reigning world champion at a classical time limit.
ideas: After d4 cxd4 cxd4 you have the classic two-pawn centre.
Black's main replies are ...d5 and ...Nf6, both hitting e4.
Far less to memorise than the Open Sicilian.

name: French: 2...d5
blurb: The French proper. Black attacks e4 and makes White decide what to do with it.
history: The point of the French Defense. Having prepared it with 1...e6, Black challenges the e4 pawn at once, and White has to decide what to do about it: advance, exchange, or defend. Each choice gives its name to a variation.
ideas: If e5, hit the base of the chain with ...c5 and pile up on d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6.
If exd5, recapture with the e-pawn and your c8 bishop is free.
If Nc3, choose between ...Nf6 and ...Bb4.

name: French: Advance Variation
blurb: White takes space and locks the centre. Black's c8 bishop stays shut in.
history:
White advances the pawn past its rival and fixes the centre. Louis Paulsen played it in the nineteenth century, but it is tied above all to Aron Nimzowitsch, who used it in his book My System to explain pawn chains and how to attack them at the base.

Black's standard plan comes straight from that lesson: strike at d4 with ...c5.
ideas: Support d4 with c3 and Nf3.
Black will attack d4 with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. Count attackers and defenders.
Your extra space gives you play on the kingside.

name: French: Exchange Variation
blurb: White releases the tension. The structure becomes symmetrical and simple.
history: White exchanges pawns and the position becomes symmetrical, with an open e-file. Paul Morphy liked it because it gave him the open game he wanted. It has a reputation as a drawing line, though with both sides free to develop easily that is not always how it turns out.
ideas: After ...exd5, develop Nf3 and Bd3, then castle.
The trade frees Black's bad bishop, so play for piece activity, not structure.
Put a rook on the open e-file.

name: Caro-Kann Defense
blurb: Like the French, Black prepares ...d5, but keeps the c8 bishop's diagonal open.
history:
Named after Horatio Caro, an English player who lived in Berlin, and Marcus Kann of Vienna, who analysed it in the 1880s. Kann won a seventeen-move game with it against Jacques Mieses at Hamburg in 1885, and Caro published his analysis the following year.

Like the French it prepares ...d5, but without shutting in the light-squared bishop. It has been the choice of solid world champions: Capablanca, Botvinnik, Petrosian and Karpov all relied on it.
ideas: Play ...d5 next.
Develop the light-squared bishop to f5 or g4 before playing ...e6.
Solid, with fewer weaknesses than most defences.

name: Caro-Kann: 2...d5
blurb: Black challenges e4 with full pawn support.
history: The move that 1...c6 prepared. Black challenges the e4 pawn with a pawn that is supported by another pawn, and White must choose between advancing, exchanging and defending, as in the French Defense. The difference is that Black's light-squared bishop is still free to come out.
ideas: If e5, play ...Bf5 and then ...e6.
If exd5, recapture with ...cxd5.
If Nc3, take with ...dxe4, then develop with ...Bf5 or ...Nf6.

name: Caro-Kann: Advance Variation
blurb: White gains space. Unlike in the French, Black's bishop gets out to f5.
history:
White advances the pawn and takes space. Mikhail Tal used it against Mikhail Botvinnik in their 1961 world championship match, but for a long time it was thought to give Black an easy game, because the bishop can come out to f5 before ...e6 is played.

It was revived in the 1990s by Nigel Short, whose quiet system with Nf3 and Be2 made it one of the main lines.
ideas: Develop Nf3 and Be2, then castle.
Black will hit your centre with ...c5.
Don't rush g4 to chase the bishop until your pieces are out.

name: Caro-Kann: Exchange Variation
blurb: A simple structure with a half-open e-file for White and a half-open c-file for Black.
history:
White exchanges pawns straight away. Following up with 4.c4 gives the Panov-Botvinnik Attack, named after Vasily Panov and Mikhail Botvinnik, which leads to open positions with an isolated d-pawn.

The quieter 4.Bd3 had a famous outing in 1970, when Bobby Fischer beat Tigran Petrosian with it in the match between the Soviet Union and the Rest of the World.
ideas: After ...cxd5, Bd3 stops ...Bf5.
c3 supports d4; Bf4 and Nf3 follow.
c4 instead leads to the sharper Panov Attack.

name: Scandinavian: 2...Qxd5
blurb: Black takes back at once. The queen is exposed, so know where it goes next.
history: The classical recapture: Black gets the pawn back at once, at the cost of bringing the queen out early. It is the move played in the oldest recorded game, in Valencia around 1475. The modern alternative is 2...Nf6, taking the pawn back with the knight instead.
ideas: After Nc3, play ...Qa5 or ...Qd6.
Then ...Nf6, ...c6 and ...Bf5.
The pawn on c6 gives your queen a retreat to c7.

name: Scandinavian: 3.Nc3
blurb: Develop with an attack on the queen. This free move is the reason to take on d5.
history: White develops a knight and attacks the queen, gaining a move. The same move was played in the game from around 1475, and it is the standard illustration of why the queen should not come out too early. Black has to decide where the queen goes next.
ideas: Then d4, Nf3 and Bc4 or Bd2.
After ...Qa5, Bd2 sets up discovered attacks on the queen.
You are a move ahead, so open the game.

name: Scandinavian: Main Line
moves: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5
blurb: The queen stays active and keeps an eye on the c3 knight.
history:
The traditional main line. From a5 the queen stays active, eyes the knight on c3 and is hard to attack again. Bent Larsen beat the world champion Anatoly Karpov with it at Montreal in 1979, and Viswanathan Anand chose it against Garry Kasparov in their 1995 title match.

The quieter retreats 3...Qd6 and 3...Qd8 have become popular alternatives.
ideas: Play ...c6 soon so the queen can drop back to c7.
Develop ...Nf6 and ...Bf5, then ...e6.
Watch for Bd2 followed by a knight move that uncovers an attack on your queen.

name: Alekhine's Defense
blurb: Black tempts the e-pawn forward, planning to attack an over-extended centre later.
history:
Named after Alexander Alekhine, later world champion, who introduced it to master play at Budapest in 1921. It is a model of the hypermodern school of that time: Black invites White's pawns forward in the hope that they will become targets.

Bobby Fischer used it twice against Boris Spassky in their 1972 world championship match, and won the thirteenth game with it.
ideas: After e5, the knight goes to d5.
Let White push pawns, then undermine them with ...d6.
You give up space, so it is risky if you don't know the plans.

name: Queen's Gambit Declined
blurb: Black holds d5 with a pawn. Solid and classical.
history:
Black declines the gambit pawn and supports the centre with ...e6 instead. It is one of the most trusted defences in chess and has been played by every world champion.

Its hold on top-level chess was at its strongest in the 1927 world championship match in Buenos Aires between José Raúl Capablanca and Alexander Alekhine, in which thirty-two of the thirty-four games were Queen's Gambits Declined.
ideas: Develop ...Nf6 and ...Be7, then castle.
The c8 bishop is shut in; ...b6 and ...Bb7 is one way to free it.
Play ...c5 when you are ready to challenge the centre.

name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
blurb: Black takes the pawn but should not try to keep it.
history:
Black accepts the pawn. The earliest writers tried to hold on to it with ...b5 and were punished for it; the modern idea is to give it back and use the time to free Black's game with ...c5.

It was a main battleground of the 1834 matches between Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais and Alexander McDonnell, the first great series of games between leading masters.
ideas: Don't defend c4 with ...b5; a4 and Qf3 tricks win material.
Use the time White spends recapturing to develop and play ...c5.
...Nf6 and ...e6 come next.

name: Slav Defense
blurb: Black supports d5 without blocking the c8 bishop.
history:
Named for the masters from Slavic countries who developed it in the 1920s and 1930s, among them Alexander Alekhine, Efim Bogoljubov and Milan Vidmar. Semyon Alapin had explored it a generation earlier.

Black supports the d5 pawn without shutting in the light-squared bishop. It was tested at length in the world championship matches between Alekhine and Max Euwe in 1935 and 1937, and it has stayed one of the main defences to the Queen's Gambit.
ideas: Bring the bishop to f5 or g4 before ...e6.
Here ...dxc4 followed by ...b5 is a real threat.
Very solid, and a natural partner to the Caro-Kann.

name: Indian Game
blurb: Black stops e4 with a piece and keeps the pawn structure flexible.
history:
The "Indian" in the names of these defences goes back to Moheschunder Bannerjee, a Bengali player whose games against the Scotsman John Cochrane in Calcutta in the 1840s and 1850s were published in Europe. He was used to Indian rules, in which a pawn could not move two squares at once, and so developed with small pawn moves and bishops on the long diagonals.

For decades these setups were thought eccentric. The hypermodern players of the 1920s, led by Aron Nimzowitsch and Richard Réti, showed that Black could control the centre with pieces from a distance, and the Indian defences became the main alternative to 1...d5.
ideas: Choose your setup next: ...e6, ...g6 or ...d5.
The knight controls e4 and d5.
Castle kingside early.

name: Indian Game: 2.c4
blurb: White takes more space and prepares Nc3 and e4.
history: The main line. White takes more space and keeps the option of putting the knight behind the c-pawn. Black's reply decides which Indian defence it will be: 2...e6 heads for the Nimzo-Indian or Queen's Indian, and 2...g6 for the King's Indian or the Grünfeld.
ideas: Nc3 next fights for e4.
Against ...g6, build the big centre with e4.
Against ...e6, Nf3 and Nc3 both work.

name: King's Indian Setup: 2...g6
blurb: Black lets White build a centre, then attacks it.
history:
Black prepares to put the bishop on g7, on the king's side, which is where the "King's" in King's Indian comes from. If Black follows with ...d6 it is the King's Indian Defense; ...d5 instead gives the Grünfeld Defense, introduced by the Austrian Ernst Grünfeld in 1922.

The King's Indian was distrusted until the 1940s, when the Soviet players Isaac Boleslavsky, David Bronstein and Efim Geller showed how much counterattack it held. It later became the fighting defence of Bobby Fischer and Garry Kasparov.
ideas: ...Bg7, ...d6 and castle, in almost any order.
Strike with ...e5 or ...c5 once you have castled.
The g7 bishop is your best piece; keep its diagonal in mind.

name: Dutch Defense
blurb: Black takes control of e4 from the side and aims for a kingside attack.
history:
Named after a book published in The Hague in 1789 by Elias Stein, who recommended 1...f5 as the best answer to 1.d4. Black takes control of e4 at the price of loosening the king's position.

Its best-known supporter was Mikhail Botvinnik, who used the Stonewall setup throughout his career, and it featured on both sides in his 1951 world championship match with David Bronstein.
ideas: ...Nf6, ...e6 and ...Be7 is the simplest setup.
The diagonal from e8 to h5 is weak; be careful about Qh5+ ideas.
Be ready for e4, the Staunton Gambit.

name: Staunton Gambit
blurb: White gives up the e-pawn to open lines against Black's weakened king.
history:
Named after Howard Staunton, the English master who was the strongest player in the world in the 1840s and who gave his name to the standard design of chess pieces. He played the gambit against Bernhard Horwitz in their match of 1846.

White gives up the e-pawn to develop quickly and attack the king's side that 1...f5 has weakened.
ideas: After ...fxe4, play Nc3 to attack the pawn.
Bg5 pins the knight that defends e4.
f3 can offer a second pawn for fast development.

name: English Opening
blurb: A flank opening. The pawn controls d5 and keeps White's centre pawns back for later.
history:
Named after the Englishman Howard Staunton, who played it in his 1843 match against Pierre Saint-Amant of France and at the London tournament of 1851. It was little used after him until the twentieth century.

Mikhail Botvinnik and Garry Kasparov made it a regular weapon, and Bobby Fischer, who had opened with the e-pawn all his life, chose it for the sixth game of his 1972 match with Boris Spassky and won one of his best games.
ideas: Nc3 and g3 with Bg2 is the standard setup.
It often becomes a Queen's Pawn opening after d4.
Slower than 1.e4; play for the d5 square.

name: English: Reversed Sicilian
blurb: A Sicilian with colours reversed. Black takes the centre.
history:
So called because the position is a Sicilian Defense with the colours reversed: White has Black's setup and an extra move in hand. The extra move matters, so Black usually plays more carefully than White does against the Sicilian.

Garry Kasparov and Anatoly Karpov contested it in several games of their 1987 world championship match in Seville.
ideas: Develop ...Nf6 and ...Nc6.
...d5 opens the game if White allows it.
White has an extra move compared with a real Sicilian, so don't over-press.

name: Réti Opening
blurb: A flexible first move. It stops ...e5 and keeps every central plan open.
history:
Named after Richard Réti, a leader of the hypermodern school of the 1920s, who held back the centre pawns and attacked the centre from the sides instead. In the strict sense the Réti Opening is 1.Nf3 d5 2.c4; the knight move on its own is also known as the Zukertort Opening.

Réti used it to beat the world champion José Raúl Capablanca at New York in 1924, Capablanca's first defeat in eight years.
ideas: Follow with d4, c4 or g3 depending on Black's reply.
It often becomes a Queen's Pawn or English opening.
You can't be hit by early tactics, but you threaten nothing yet either.

name: Van't Kruijs Opening: 1...e5
blurb: White's quiet first move asks nothing. Take the centre.
history:
Named after Maarten van 't Kruijs, a leading Dutch player of the nineteenth century from Amsterdam, who liked to begin with this modest pawn move. It commits White to very little and often turns into another opening.

Taking the centre with 1...e5 is Black's most natural reply. If White follows with d4, the game can become a French Defense with the colours reversed.
ideas: Follow with ...d5 for a full pawn centre.
Develop the knights to f6 and c6.
If d4 hits your centre, defend with ...Nc6 or push ...e4.
